items.title: Inserting an order into a shuffle sum lowers its back-and-forth rank by two
items.author: David Gonzalez; Dino Rossegger
items.work: Scott sentence complexities of linear orderings
items.difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author labelled lemma at source0.tex lines 1024-1027: for a shuffle sum A and an order B of the form L times Q, a rank alpha comparison between A and B upgrades to a rank alpha plus two comparison between A plus L plus B and A plus B. The statement is a rank shift that says nothing about how the extra two moves are spent, and the proof (source lines 1028-1056) has to exhibit the strategy explicitly: the existential player first copies the opponent tuple through isomorphisms of the outer parts, which leaves exactly one non-isomorphic interval, then uses that the remainders of a shuffle sum are again shuffle sums to move the comparison onto the two orders themselves, then on the following turn answers inside the inserted order by identifying its initial segment with the remainder of the first order, and finally reduces the goal to the hypothesis through the self-similarity of a shuffle sum. The whole argument is a two-move strategy in the back-and-forth game, and the statement contains none of it.

proof_spans.label: the complete author proof of lem:shufflesum, retained line for line

contexts.label: author definition of the shuffle sum of a set of countable linear orders, and the remark that an order of the form L times Q is a special case (source lines 1016-1023), retained as context because the counted statement and proof use both
